LEAF & LINEAGE · OCTOBER 22, 2026

A fairer push.
A steadier family line.

Pattern Lab’s battle and strength-breeding audit. The tests found and corrected weak muscle forces, excessive turning influence, unhelpful circling, and large mutation-free strength swings.

25,840final simulated matches

Strength helps. It does not pick the winner.

With all other traits fixed, high-strength beetles won 135 matches and lost 67; 278 drew. That is 66.8% of the decisive matches. Speed helped approaching and circling, without becoming extra muscle force.

PoolMatchesStronger beetle won*Faster beetle won*Draws
48 varied founders2,40055.4%47.5%39.4%
96 children + 48 grandchildren2,40052.2%45.3%36.8%

*Among non-draw matches where the compared trait differs. Tied speed values are excluded from that column. These mixed-genome percentages describe a sampled pool, not the effect of changing that trait alone.

Better strength, grip, attention, tactics and endurance have measurable effects. Heavy bodies resist shoves but turn and accelerate more slowly. Bracing helps head-on contact while slowing turns; sideways balance protects side contact. These are situational advantages, not universal win bonuses.

Close matches still draw: about 38.1% of the mixed-genome games. Identical opponents draw more often. The audit does not promise that every design is equally effective.

Babies grow stronger or weaker gradually.

Strength is now a continuous breeding-value approximation representing many small genetic effects. Each parent contributes near its own current strength. Without mutation, a baby is at most 3.47 unrounded points from the parents’ average; about 95% were within 1.92 points. A child can be slightly stronger or weaker than both similar-strength parents.

Mutation per contributionBabies95% within parent average ±Changes over 10 pointsWithout strength mutation
0%20,0001.92 points0 (0.000%)0
0.5% (default)30,0001.99 points16 (0.053%)0
3%30,0002.15 points106 (0.353%)0

Normal strength mutations are small. Five percent of strength-mutation events use a larger effect, in either direction; the classroom mutation setting controls how often those events happen. At the default 0.5% rate, this batch had 16 changes over 10 points in 30,000 babies—roughly one in 1875. Every such change had a recorded strength mutation.

Selecting the strongest or weakest two offspring from 20 babies over 30 generations, with mutation off, moved the parents’ average from 50.5 to 97.0 or 1.0. Improvement remains possible through repeated selection.

This strength model is deliberately different from a literal single Mendelian gene. Existing beetles keep their stored strength. New births use the gradual rule. Color, pattern and the other simple loci still inherit actual parental copies. This is an invented educational model, not measured beetle physiology.

What changed in the arena

  • A sustained push moves the touching pair in the winning force’s direction; it no longer kicks both beetles apart.
  • Walking speed supplies approach and circling. Muscle, grip, alignment, energy and defensive support determine sustained pushing.
  • Tactics predicts movement and seeks the inner side of an opponent before pushing toward the edge.
  • Off-center shoves can turn a defender; mass and sideways balance resist that turn.
  • Both beetles make decisions from the same start-of-step movement state. Identical-beetle tests produced 760 red wins and 803 blue wins, with 2437 draws across 4,000 matches.
  • Old SUMO2 notebook records replay under their original rules. New shared matches require matching SUMO3 rules on both screens.

How to reproduce the checks

Use the repository’s tools/audit-battles.cjs and tools/audit-strength.cjs. Final battle seeds use offset 17342991, separate from calibration seeds. The runs cover 20 controlled traits, five levels each of strength and speed, 21 profile matchups, 48 founders, 96 children, 48 grandchildren and four identical-genome corner controls. Games use the production simulation at 60 fixed steps per simulated second. Separate regression checks cover force direction, meaningful strength, approach speed, endurance, bracing, saved genes, mutation bounds, gradual selection and legacy replays.

These finite tests show that the model behaves as intended in the sampled cases. They cannot prove perfect balance for every possible genome. No student data was used.
